# Genesis 22 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of Sources Consulted

I was able to draw from Enduring Word (David Guzik, Pentecostal/charismatic), Bible.org (evangelical), Gill's Exposition (older Baptist), Ellicott's Commentary (Anglican), Spurgeon (Reformed Baptist), and Desiring God (John Piper, Reformed Baptist). I was unable, due to search limits, to fetch full pages from Lutheran, Catholic/Orthodox, or modern scholarship sites. Below, everything is attributed to what was actually read.

---

## v. 1 — "Some time later God tested Abraham…"

*   **"After these things"** — The events of Genesis 21 (Isaac's birth and weaning, Ishmael's expulsion, the covenant with Abimelech) had concluded. Abraham was enjoying a season of peace before this sudden trial (Ellicott). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-22.html

*   **"God tested Abraham"** — The Hebrew *nacah/nasah* means "to prove or try," not to tempt toward sin. This was a test to *reveal* faith God had built over decades, not to produce new faith (Guzik). Gill notes that Jewish tradition counted this as the tenth and final of Abraham's trials, and that had Abraham slain Isaac it would not have been sin because it was by God's direct command as Lord of life. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-22/ ; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/22.htm

*   **The Divine name "Elohim"** — Bible.org notes that "Elohim" (not YHWH) is used here; critical scholars use the alternation of divine names to argue for multiple documentary sources, but the rabbis explain the distinction theologically: Elohim represents God's power as Creator, and YHWH His covenant mercies. — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-22

*   **"Here I am"** — The Hebrew idiom "Behold me" (*hinneh*) expresses readiness to be taught, to obey, and to surrender (Guzik). It is an idiom of availability used also in Exodus 3:4 and Isaiah 6:8 (Bible.org). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-22/ ; https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-22

*   **Spurgeon** preached that this test was the severest of Abraham's trials: "I cannot imagine a greater test than that which the Lord applied to Abraham. The Jews usually say that Abraham was tried ten times. Surely on this occasion he was tried ten times in one." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-22/ (citing Spurgeon)

---

## v. 2 — "Take your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love…"

*   **The escalating description** — God's command piles up terms of endearment: "your son," "your only son," "whom you love," then finally "Isaac." Each phrase was "like a knife" to Abraham's heart (Guzik). Ellicott notes the Hebrew is more emphatic: "Take, I pray, thy son, thine only son, whom thou lovest, even Isaac." The word "now" is not an adverb of time but an interjection of entreaty. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-22/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-22.html

*   **"Your only son"** — Though Abraham also had Ishmael, he had been sent away (Gen 21:8-14). As far as God's covenant was concerned, Abraham had only one son (Guzik). Gill explains Isaac was the "only legitimate son," the only son of the promise through Sarah. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-22/ ; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/22.htm

*   **First mention of love in the Bible** — Guzik highlights that from Genesis 1:1 onward, this is the first appearance of the word "love," and it comes in the context of a father's love for his son, connected with sacrificial offering — a foreshadowing of the Father giving the Son. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-22/

*   **"The land of Moriah"** — Ellicott notes two possible meanings: "Jah is teacher" (supported by Isaiah 2:3) or "Jah is provider" (which fits vv. 8 and 14). Bible.org lists several ancient translations: the Vulgate and Samaritan Pentateuch render it "visions," the Targums as "worship," the Septuagint as "high." The more probable meaning is "the place of appearing." 2 Chronicles 3:1 identifies Mount Moriah as the site of the Temple. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-22.html ; https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-22

*   **"Offer him there as a burnt offering"** — The Hebrew term *'olah* means a sacrifice wholly consumed by fire. The animal was first slain, then cut into pieces, arranged on the wood, and burned entirely (Guzik, Gill). This is not a "spiritual" offering; Hengstenberg's argument that Abraham was only to "surrender Isaac spiritually" is contradicted by the narrative itself and by Hebrews 11:17-19 (Ellicott). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-22/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-22.html

*   **Pagan context** — Guzik notes that the Canaanite priests believed their gods demanded human sacrifice. Abraham might have initially wondered if Yahweh was like those pagan gods. By the end of the story, God demonstrates He is the opposite — He does not want human sacrifice. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-22/

*   **Seeming contradiction with the promise** — God had promised "in Isaac your seed shall be called" (Gen 21:12). The command appeared to require Abraham to destroy the very promise God had made him. Guzik writes: "Abraham had to learn the difference between trusting the promise and trusting the Promiser." Spurgeon adds: "It is neither your business nor mine to fulfill God's promise, nor to do the least wrong to produce the greatest good." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-22/

---

## v. 3 — "So Abraham got up early the next morning…"

*   **Immediate obedience** — There is no record of argument, hesitation, or questioning. Spurgeon: "But there is not a word of argument; not one solitary question that even looks like hesitation. 'God is God,' he seems to say, and it is not for me to ask him why." Bible.org notes the text records no hesitation, though it must have been a sleepless night. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-22/ ; https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-22

*   **Abraham did the work himself** — Even as a wealthy sheik, Abraham personally saddled his donkey and split the wood. Spurgeon: "He was a sheik and a mighty man in his camp, but he became a wood-splitter, thinking no work menial if done for God, and reckoning the work too sacred for other hands. With splitting heart he cleaves the wood." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-22/

*   **Ellicott** notes that Abraham took wood already cleft (split), not because there was no wood at the destination (v. 13 shows there was a thicket), but so that on arrival nothing would distract — they could proceed at once to the sacrifice. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-22.html

---

## v. 4 — "On the third day Abraham looked up and saw the place in the distance."

*   **Three days of silent suffering** — The distance from Beersheba to Mount Moriah is about 40-45 miles, roughly a two-and-a-half to three-day journey (Bible.org, Ellicott). Spurgeon captures the agony: "To be burnt quick to death upon the blazing fagot is comparatively an easy martyrdom, but to hang in chains roasting at a slow fire, to have the heart hour by hour pressed as in a vice, this it is that trieth faith; and this it was that Abraham endured through three long days." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-22/ ; https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-22

*   **Typology of the third day** — The Jewish commentators noted the significance of the third day and linked it to Hosea 6:2 ("on the third day He will raise us up"). Gill writes that "from the time that Abraham had the command to offer up his son, he was reckoned no other by him than as one dead, from whence he received him in a figure on this third day" (Hebrews 11:19). This prefigures Christ's resurrection on the third day (Guzik, Gill). — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/22.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-22/

*   **"Saw the place afar off"** — Ellicott notes that Mount Moriah cannot be seen from a distance greater than about three miles by a traveller from Beersheba. This fits the geography: Abraham left the servants at that spot, and Isaac carried the wood the remaining three miles on foot. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-22.html

*   Jewish tradition (cited by Gill) held that Abraham saw a cloud of glory or a pillar of fire on the mount, identifying it as the designated place. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/22.htm

---

## v. 5 — "Stay here with the donkey … The boy and I will go over there to worship, and then we will return to you."

*   **First use of "worship"** — Guzik notes this is the first occurrence of the word "worship" (*shachah*, "to bow down") in reference to God in Scripture. Abraham and Isaac went to bow down, not to have a time of joyful praise. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-22/

*   **"We will come back to you"** — Abraham did not merely say "I will come back." He said "we." Hebrews 11:17-19 explains that Abraham "concluded that God was able to raise him up, even from the dead." Abraham had no precedent in Biblical history for resurrection, yet his faith rested in God's ability to keep His promise (Guzik). Ellicott adds that belief in resurrection was "no new thing with Abraham, as it was part of the creed both of Chaldea and Egypt." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-22/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-22.html

*   Bible.org notes the four Hebrew cohortatives: "stay here," "we will go," "we will worship," "we will return" — all expressing Abraham's settled determination. — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-22

---

## v. 6 — "Abraham took the wood … and placed it on his son Isaac. He himself carried the fire and the sacrificial knife."

*   **Isaac as a type of Christ** — The Fathers of the church discerned in Isaac carrying his own wood a type of Christ carrying His cross (Ellicott, citing John 19:17). Guzik likewise notes the picture: the son of promise, carrying the wood of his own sacrifice up the hill, in willing obedience to his father. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-22.html ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-22/

*   **The fire and the knife** — The knife (*ma'akelet*) was a large butcher's knife used for cooking purposes (Bible.org, citing Judges 19:29 and Proverbs 30:14). Spurgeon said: "That knife was cutting into his own heart all the while, yet he took it. Unbelief would have left the knife at home, but genuine faith takes it." — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-22 ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-22/

*   **"The two of them walked on together"** — This literally means "they went in agreement." The phrase is repeated in v. 8 for emphasis. Both father and son were united in purpose (Guzik). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-22/

---

## v. 7 — "The fire and the wood are here … but where is the lamb for the burnt offering?"

*   **Isaac's innocent question** — Isaac perceived by the fire and wood that a burnt offering was intended, but noticed no animal. Guzik says this question must have "cut Abraham to the heart." The fact that Isaac understood the elements of sacrifice shows that sacrificial worship predates the Mosaic legislation (Bible.org, citing Cain and Abel, Noah, and Job). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-22/ ; https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-22

*   **"My father … Here I am, my son"** — The exchange of these tender terms emphasizes the mutual love between father and son. Guzik notes that the text highlights the love and respect both held for each other. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-22/

---

## v. 8 — "God Himself will provide the lamb for the burnt offering, my son."

*   **A prophetic statement** — Guzik explains that Abraham did not yet know *how* God would provide; he still trusted that God could raise Isaac from the dead. Yet his words proved prophetic. The question "Where is the lamb?" was asked by all the faithful from Isaac to Moses to David to Isaiah — until John the Baptist answered by pointing to Jesus: "the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world" (John 1:29). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-22/

*   **"God will provide" (Elohim Yireh)** — This phrase later becomes the name "Jehovah Jireh" in v. 14. The Hebrew verb literally means "to see" and came to mean "to see to it," i.e., "to provide" (Bible.org). Gill suggests Abraham may have had in view the Messiah, "the Lamb of God … whom He had provided in council and covenant before the world was." — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-22 ; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/22.htm

*   Ellicott suggests Abraham "meant Isaac by the lamb, thus showing that it was not he who chose the victim, but God." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-22.html

*   **"So the two of them walked on together"** — The repetition from v. 6. Gill cites the Targum of Jonathan: "they went both of them with a perfect heart as one," and Jarchi: "with a like heart" — suggesting Isaac understood and consented. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/22.htm

---

## v. 9 — "Abraham built the altar … bound his son Isaac and placed him on the altar."

*   **Abraham built the altar** — Gill notes the Jewish tradition that this was the very spot where David and Solomon later built the altar (the threshing floor of Araunah), where Noah built his altar after the flood, and where Adam offered after creation. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/22.htm

*   **"Bound his son Isaac"** — The Hebrew verb for "bind" (*'aqad*) occurs only here in the Old Testament. The root means "to bend or twist," referring to the twisting of a sacrificial animal's legs to tie them together (Bible.org). Jewish commentators agree it was done with Isaac's consent; he could have resisted (Ellicott). Guzik notes that Abraham was over 100 years old and Isaac could have escaped easily had he chosen to. Isaac's faith, submitting willingly, is part of the picture. — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-22 ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-22.html ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-22/

*   **Isaac's age** — Jewish tradition varies. Some say he was about 5 (after weaning), others 13, 25 (Josephus), 26, or 36-37 (Targum of Jonathan). Spurgeon thought possibly "five-and-twenty — so Josephus thinks — possibly thirty-three years of age, and, if so, very manifestly the type of Christ, who was about that age when he came to die." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/22.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-22/

*   Guzik lists the deliberate, slow-motion detail: "came to the place … built an altar … laid the wood in order … bound Isaac … laid him on the altar." The narrative conveys the weight and drama of every action. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-22/

---

## v. 10 — "Abraham reached out his hand and took the knife to slaughter his son."

*   **No mere drama** — Abraham fully intended to go through with it. Spurgeon: "Notice the obedience of this friend of God – it was no playing at giving up his son: it was really doing it. It was no talking about what he could do, and would do, perhaps, but his faith was practical and heroic." Gill says the knife was near Isaac's throat, "and in another moment, as it were, it would have been all over." God took the will for the deed. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-22/ ; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/22-10.htm

*   Guzik elaborates: "God often takes the will for the deed with His people. When He finds them truly willing to make the sacrifice He demands, God often does not require it. This is how believers can be martyrs without ever dying for Jesus." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-22/

---

## vv. 11-12 — "The angel of the LORD called … 'Do not lay a hand on the boy … now I know that you fear God.'"

*   **"The Angel of the LORD"** — The text identifies this angel as speaking in the first person as God: "you have not withheld your only son from Me." This is understood as a theophany — a pre-incarnate appearance of God the Son (Guzik). Bible.org notes the difficulty: the angel refers to "God" in the third person yet speaks as God. This is one of several passages in Genesis that hint at plurality within the Godhead (along with "Let us" in Gen 1:26, the Spirit in Gen 1:2, etc.). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-22/ ; https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-22

*   **"Abraham, Abraham!"** — The double calling of the name signals urgency. The Septuagint doubles the address in v. 1 as well, but the Hebrew text has it only here in v. 11 (Bible.org). — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-22

*   **"Now I know that you fear God"** — This does not imply God lacked foreknowledge. Bible.org says, "I understand it … as a literary way of showing approval to Abraham's faith. I am uncomfortable with Open Theism." Ellicott's earlier comments align: God "proved" Abraham, putting his faith to the test, but not to learn something God did not already know — rather to make Abraham's faith manifest. — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-22 ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-22.html

*   **"Fear God"** — This term can mean "fear," "awe," "respect," or "honor" depending on context. Bible.org notes it is a lifestyle relationship: "Obedience flows from respect and love, not fear of reprisal." — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-22

*   **God's rejection of human sacrifice** — Guzik emphasizes that God here emphatically demonstrated He was not like the pagan gods. "God strongly and clearly demonstrated that He did not want human sacrifice." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-22/

---

## v. 13 — "Abraham looked up and saw … a ram in a thicket, caught by its horns."

*   **The substitutionary ram** — Ellicott declares: "We have here the fact of substitution, and the doctrine of a vicarious sacrifice. The ram took Isaac's place, and by its actual death completed the typical representation of the Saviour's death on Calvary." He explains that the "two-part" representation (Isaac spared, the ram slain) teaches that "what was wanting in Isaac should be supplied by the ram" — life springing from a substitute's death. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-22.html

*   **"Behind him"** — Ellicott notes a textual variant: many ancient authorities read "one ram" (*'echad*) instead of "a ram behind" (*'achar*), by a slight change in one consonant. This correction is "almost certain" since "behind" is not used elsewhere as an adverb of place. The ram was probably the type with four horns still common in the Middle East. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-22.html

*   **"In place of his son"** — This substitutionary act is "the incipient form of sacrifice as the substitutionary act … later developed, not only in the Mosaic legislation, but also supremely in the sacrifice of Christ" (Bible.org, referencing Isaiah 53 and the book of Hebrews). — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-22

---

## v. 14 — "Abraham called that place The LORD Will Provide."

*   **Jehovah Jireh** — The name means "YHWH will see" or "YHWH will provide." Guzik notes that Abraham did not name the place "Mount Trial," "Mount Agony," or "Mount Obedience," but "Mount Provision" — focusing on what God did, not what Abraham experienced. Spurgeon: "Abraham says nothing about himself at all, but the praise is unto God … 'Jehovah will provide.' I like that self-ignoring." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-22/

*   **Proverbial saying** — Ellicott discusses the phrase "In the mount of the LORD it shall be provided" (or "it shall be seen"). The Septuagint reads "In the mount the LORD shall be seen," which would be a prophecy of Christ's manifestation. The Samaritan, Syriac, and Vulgate read "In the mount the LORD will provide." Ellicott adds that the proverb "is a national testimony to the genuineness of the record, and proves that the facts narrated in it were so impressed upon the memory of Abraham's descendants, as to shape their thoughts and language." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-22.html

*   **Pointing to Calvary** — Guzik says Abraham knew God would provide the ultimate sacrifice on that very hill someday. Spurgeon adds: "God provided a ram instead of Isaac. This was sufficient for the occasion as a type; but that which was typified by the ram is infinitely more glorious. In order to save us God provided God. I cannot put it more simply. He did not provide an angel, nor a mere man, but God himself." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-22/

---

## vv. 15-16 — "The angel of the LORD called … a second time … 'By Myself I have sworn, declares the LORD.'"

*   **God swears by Himself** — This is the only instance in Genesis where God swears by Himself (Bible.org). Ellicott calls it "this solemn interposition of an oath (Hebrews 6:17), of which the present is the sole instance in Holy Scripture." The blessing now differs from earlier promises: (1) it is no longer a bare promise but a "solemn compact ratified by an oath," (2) it assures Abraham's seed of victory over enemies, and (3) it transfers to Abraham's offspring the promise of being the means of blessing to all nations. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-22.html ; https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-22

*   Guzik notes the voice is in the first person — "By Myself I have sworn" — suggesting Jesus the Messiah, God the Son, was uniquely present. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-22/

---

## v. 17 — "I will surely bless you, and I will multiply your descendants like the stars … and the sand."

*   **Intensified promises** — The Hebrew uses double grammatical constructions for emphasis: the Piel infinitive absolute with the Piel imperfect ("I will greatly bless you") and the Hiphil infinitive absolute with the Hiphil imperfect ("I will greatly multiply"). This goes back to the original promises of Genesis 12 (Bible.org). — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-22

*   Guzik notes that, by rough calculation, the number of stars in the sky and grains of sand on the seashore are approximately the same: 10 to the 25th power (citing Henry Morris). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-22/

*   **"Possess the gates of their enemies"** — To seize the gate was to capture the city itself. Bible.org notes that the same metaphor appears in Matthew 16: "the gates of hell shall not overcome the church." — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-22

---

## v. 18 — "Through your offspring all nations of the earth will be blessed, because you have obeyed My voice."

*   **The Messianic promise reaffirmed** — The promise first given in Genesis 12:3 is repeated and confirmed. Bible.org discusses the grammatical issue of whether the Niphal/Hithpael form of "bless" should be translated passively ("shall be blessed") or reflexively ("shall bless themselves"). The NT quotes (Acts 3:25, Galatians 3:8) use the passive. — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-22

*   **Obedience as the ground** — The text says "because you have obeyed My voice." Bible.org notes this shows "the unconditional/conditional nature of the covenants of the Bible … related to God's unconditional love, but human's conditional response." — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-22

---

## v. 19 — "Abraham went back to his servants … and settled in Beersheba."

*   **The return** — Notably, only Abraham is mentioned returning to the servants. Isaac is not explicitly named, though the implication is that they "went together." Guzik suggests the narrative silence may highlight that Isaac was now a man "risen from the dead" in a figurative sense, dedicated afresh to God. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-22/

---

## vv. 20-24 — The genealogy of Nahor's family, including Rebekah.

*   **Purpose of the genealogy** — At first glance this seems an odd placement, but Ellicott explains the news of Nahor's descendants "was the cause probably of Abraham's determination to seek a wife for his son from among his own kindred" (which becomes the subject of Genesis 24). Bible.org concurs: it "lays the groundwork for Isaac's future bride, Rebekah." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-22.html ; https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-22

*   **Twelve sons** — Ellicott observes a pattern: Nahor has twelve sons (eight by his wife, four by his concubine), just as Jacob later has twelve sons (eight by two wives, four by two concubines), and Ishmael has twelve sons. He dismisses the claim that such coincidences prove the narratives are mythical: "coincidences quite as strange are to be found in every history, and in daily life." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-22.html

*   **Individual names** — Ellicott notes that Uz (Huz) may be connected to the land of Uz (Job 1:1); Buz may be the ancestor of Elihu (Job 32:2); Kemuel ("father of Aram") is ancestor of the family of Ram (Elihu's lineage), not the Aramaic race; Chesed may be the ancestor of the Chaldean raiders who plundered Job (Job 1:17); Maacah appears as a small Aramaic people in Deuteronomy 3:14 and 2 Samuel 10:6. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-22.html

*   **Rebekah** — The name possibly means "to tie up an animal" and by extension "an ensnaring one." The rabbis saw this as referring to her enticing beauty (Bible.org). She will become Isaac's wife and the mother of Jacob and Esau. — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/genesis-22

---

## Brief Note on Traditions and Distinctives

Because of search limits I was unable to fetch full pages from specifically Lutheran (LCMS, 1517.org), Catholic/Orthodox (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org), or modern scholarship (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org) sites. However, from what emerged in the searches:

*   **Reformed/Presbyterian** — Not directly accessed, but the Desiring God (Piper) article emphasizes that the Abraham-Isaac event was historically unique and unrepeatable, designed to inaugurate a paradigm shift away from human sacrifice and to typologically foreshadow Christ. This is broadly the Reformed reading. — https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/abraham-take-your-son

*   **Baptist** — Spurgeon (Reformed Baptist) and Gill (older Baptist) represent the traditional Baptist reading: strong emphasis on faith demonstrated by works (cf. James 2:21-23), individual obedience, and the typological foreshadowing of Christ. Spurgeon's sermons especially dwell on the "heroic" nature of Abraham's practical faith. — https://www.ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons15.xxii.html

*   **Pentecostal/Charismatic** — Enduring Word (David Guzik) represents this tradition. The commentary does not differ markedly from evangelical readings but emphasizes personal application, the voice of God, and the power of faith to act on God's word even when it contradicts circumstances. The "third day" resurrection typology is stressed. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-22/

*   **Methodist/Wesleyan/Holiness** — No sources were directly fetched from seedbed.com or wesley.nnu.edu; these traditions would typically emphasize the "testing" as sanctifying, perfecting Abraham's love and fear of God.

*   **Anglican** — Ellicott's Commentary (1878), an Anglican work, represents the traditional Protestant reading of the passage with careful attention to the Hebrew text, typology (Isaac as type of Christ), and the doctrinal significance of substitutionary atonement. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-22.html

*   **Catholic and Orthodox** — Not directly accessed, but the early Church Fathers (referenced by Ellicott) consistently saw Isaac carrying the wood as a type of Christ carrying the cross. The phrase "your only son" is read typologically as pointing to Christ as the "only-begotten" Son. The Orthodox Study Bible (OCA tradition) reads the binding of Isaac as a type of the Crucifixion and the ram as a type of Christ's substitutionary sacrifice.

*   **Modern scholarship** — Not directly accessed, but Bible.org's notes mention that critical scholars of the 18th-19th centuries used the alternation of Elohim/YHWH to postulate a documentary hypothesis. Bible.org rejects this in favor of the rabbinic theological explanation for the divine names. Further modern scholarly views (e.g., from netbible.org or bibleodyssey.org) would address the cultural context of child sacrifice in the ancient Near East and the narrative's function as an etiological rejection of the practice.
